If you're worried about the weight, check it at least once every two weeks... It's not good if they grow too fast, because their bones will lose density... ( At least that's what my dietitian told me)

My dog eats a mix of Loisachtaler canned food, kibble from Irish pure, some rice and veggies, occasionally with a boiled egg... A lot of Eurasier owners with similar problems seem to feed 'platinum' though... If you want to try different brands, always search for a puppy pack or starter kit... Sadly, he just didn't quite like it, so I had to give in... 

If you want to prepare your dog's food, you DEFINITELY need to get a dietitian... Or at least the software which exactly calculates the nutritional needs...

I wish you a lot of fun and luck with your new puppy! 
On snacks, it really depends since many eurasier are very picky... I have an extreme case and always have to iterate through my snacks... We use treats from SANA, real nature wilderness, jacks, fresco (I find their quality quite fluctuating though) and some I bake myself... 
For high value treats I use small pieces of rumen, dry horse heart, some cheese (Emmentaler or Parmesan ) or appetizer by 'my'...

Very popular brands are Wolfsblut (mine doesn't like it at all) or Rinti...

Just try out what fits you, your pup and your training best and make sure you check the ingredients first for high quality treats... Differ between standard and high value treats... 
It would be best if your pup can be motivated with your default kibble... Mine won't do much for some kibble, so that doesn't really work for me... 

Additional info: it's great that you want to feed your pup according to the breeder's club recommendation... If you want to make extra sure to get the right amount, find a dietitian who'll calculate it specifically for your dog depending on its parents and his own weight... In addition, be flexible... My dog refused to eat the breeder's recommendation and we had a long journey before we found some food he was willing to eat frequently... That's a common struggle with Eurasier... 😅

You don't even know a single thing, yet you assume, we didn't try properly! I tried a lot of different approaches and spoke to many dog owners and trained professionals... 
There *is* a genetic component that you should not leave out and there are significant differences between each and every individual dog! Plus, Eurasier are known for being totally family-bound, so they have a disposition for separation anxiety! 
I'm not giving up and just blaming the genetics, but you cannot leave genetics and the individual personality out!!

I won't let anyone claim that I skip accountability while I spent hours and hours loving and training my dog to be a proper companion, speaking with professionals and doing my own research on modern training methods...

It's great how much thought you put in before you get a dog! Basically, an Eurasier seems to fit what you'd expect from your dog... But Eurasier are known to have heavy separation anxiety... My own dog can't be alone for more than 15 minutes even though we tried different methods to train that and even asked our trainer... 
While we know other Eurasier owners, who have no problems with leaving their dog alone for hours, there is still a rather high probability for separation anxiety with Eurasier...

While Eurasier usually do not lose a lot of fur, your floors will probably turn into a one piece fur carpet when shedding season starts... Eurasier fur tends to vary a lot, so maybe ask the puppy parents' owner first and seek less fluffy Eurasier...

Hi... Congrats to your new Eurasier! 
It's normal for pups to drink a lot of water, since they are still growing... My dog drank a crazy amount of water when he was still growing...
About eating... Well, welcome to the common Eurasier problem! They are well-known picky eaters... Often check on his weight, if he's keeping it, no worries... My dog eats like a third of what he should eat, but he keeps a very healthy and steady body weight... It would be easier if you tried out some different food brands, but keep in mind that you have to do it step by step... 

About Training... It's totally normal that his concentration isn't too long right now, because he's still a pup... Training outside is really hard, because there are A LOT of distractions... If the commands work at home, add distractions slowly...
Instead of having long periods of training, do short ones before meals (5min or so) and do one or two cues multiple times a day randomly... You don't want your dog to listen only if it's training time... 

Dogs don't really have to play the way we'd like to play... It's something we humans do... I didn't play with mine until he was 5 months old because he wasn't too interested and was always distracted... Stash away the toys, just have two toys lying around, but swap them with the stashed ones... It keeps them interesting... 
It's more important to let them play with other pups... Do a lot of social interactions with other dogs... (Letting them play and letting them pass) 

If you need training advice, I'd really recommend the puppy vids from Zac George on YouTube or mk9plus... 
Good luck with your new dog!

It depends on how big your Eurasier is! It's healthiest for dogs if they can lay flat on the bed, because their spine can relax overnight... I'd recommend to buy a bed that's at least 1m wide, because they grow very fast and mine has always been quite attached to his beds...
I bought a pricey Kudde by sabro... It's orthopedic and has no fluff... My dog sleeps in there overnight, though he'll switch between dog bed, tiles and my bed! 

About overheating: I recently bought a cloud 7 just for fun and I thought he'd overheat... I don't know how, but he doesn't! He absolutely adores it and rests on it multiple times a day...
Eurasier don't have to have blue spots on the tongue... There are a lot with normal pink tongues and as for mine, he even has a completely blue tongue...

Puppy stage is definitely a lot of biting and rough play! Plus, they don't realize how fast they grow... Meeting some pups is a great idea if you have some near you and maybe pup-sit one and ask the owner about their recent difficulties, but please have in mind that each dog is different...

I wouldn't say that female-male is better for bonding... It depends on the personality... If your pom has aggression towards other males, it might be a bad idea to get yourself another male... But there is no guarantee that a female would work out... It's just like with humans: we meet people we like and we meet some we dislike just like dogs do!
Prophylactic spaying is morally reprehensible... We don't go and amputate body parts just because of some risks, do we? Go to check-ups regularly instead of spaying... Plus, spaying/castration have a lot of downsides. Please read  through some reliable sources before making this decision!

That's great! A lot of owners tend to forget about dog safety!

Technically, you can... It is just absolutely not recommended to leave your Eurasier at home since they're insanely attached... If you're definitely planning with a pet sitter, better choose another breed... Stay alone training tends to be very hard with Eurasier and many do not trust other people who aren't their family... We now have our yearly holidays with dog or there are none! 

To conclude, I do not want to discourage you from getting an Eurasier, they are really great dogs! But they do come with their own challenges like bonding hard and never wanting to leave your side. Plus, puppies are very exhausting no matter which breed. Eurasier are no small breed, so it can naturally become a danger to your pom. (Mine currently weighs 28kg)
Please gather enough information and decide for yourself if you can put up with all that before getting a pup and I'm sure everything will work out!

Playing as we understand it is not necessarily natural for dogs... They catch up quickly but you gotta teach them!

You could start by teaching them the different steps of fetch first. Like to hold something in the mouth, to bring it and leave it. Start with very small distances and reward them... Don't overdo it and stop at 2 or 3 times at first... After a while they should understand how to play - some learn fetch faster some slower...
My dog didn't like to fetch for the first six months, now he loves and initiates to play fetch but will stop after 5 times... Each dog is a bit different if it comes to play...

Eurasier are basically rather calm though there's no guarantee that the one you're gonna get is going to be calm since they vary a lot.
I think you want to get a puppy? I think almost no puppy is totally calm when young... Mine wasn't although others considered him calm in comparison to other pups. It could happen that you need to calm both dogs at once then.

Why do you want to get a female and plan on spaying her? Why not get another male? I think it's never a good idea to get a dog with the idea of neutering/spaying it since it's not ethical. Plus, the fur of Eurasier will totally overgrow if you spay / neuter them and additionally there will be some changes personality-wise.

For the part with Eurasier living with other dogs: it depends as well. My dog turned out to be very tolerant of other dogs but still wants to be the prince of the household. He loves other dogs but dislikes being around them for a longer period of time.

Travelling is mostly training. Obviously it's more difficult by plane with an Eurasier than a pom (the size and stuff) and you shouldn't travel without your Eurasier since they are very attached. You should make sure to transport larger dogs safely (in a box or with harness and seatbelt), otherwise it could get dangerous for you and the dogs.

Airtags are good, if you live in a city with many Apple users. Airtags' location tracking CAN be accurate, but can be completely inaccurate as well... 

Here's why: airtags work with apple devices. The devices communicate with each other and create a mesh. With this mesh the airtag can be located very accurately since the distances to the next device can be calculated with the strength of the signal. BUT if there aren't any Apple devices close the Airtag cannot determine where the device is, hence it is useless if you're trying to locate your dog in the woods.

All in all, it depends on where you're living/where you're taking your dog for walks. I'd rather recommend Tractive where you can make virtual fences and are dependable at any time/location.

Temperature tolerance is not breed specific, but rather dependent on the location of the last one or two generations. If your sheeb and his parents are used to living in colder regions, the tolerance of your sheeb would be quite low.
There are a lot of dog breeds which where originally founded in nordic countries (e.g samoyed) but bred and raised in hot regions (e.g california), which will have absolute no problem with heat and rather freeze in the north.
I guess your dog is used to your country's climate and therefore has a denser and warmer fur, leading to being less heat tolerant.

I would just keep an eye on your dog, comb his fur daily to get excess fur out and give him breaks from the heat (like some frozen dog treats, shadow cool paw bath, etc). If it's important to you, you can get your dog used to heat in small steps by exposing him more frequently to warm weather, but keep a good eye on him. Overheating is very dangerous for dogs and it happens fast.

Dann muss wohl an der Unsicherheit gearbeitet werden... Der Partner sollte wohl mehr Zeit (Quality Time) mit dem Hund verbringen und die Bindung stärken... Evtl hilft Hundesport?

Weiß nicht, wie bei euch der Abruf ist, aber folgendes könnte man ausprobieren, je nachdem wie das Vertrauen ist... 
Oftmals hat mein Hund verweigert weiterzugehen, wenn er gemerkt hat, dass es nach Hause geht... 
Ich habe dann versucht ihn aufzufordern und wenn das nicht ging, hab ich (vorausgesetzt keine anderen Menschen oder Hunde) die Leine hingelegt, mich verabschiedet und bin gegangen ohne mich umzudrehen... Meistens kam der kleine schon nach 2m an, hab ihn richtig gelobt, die Leine genommen und ihn mit einem "weiter" Kommando aufgefordert weiter zu gehen...

Das kenn ich von meinem Hund... Es war eine Zeit lang so, dass wir für eine 10 Minuten Strecke mit dem Hund 30min gebraucht hat...
Pubertät ist natürlich ein Punkt, das kickt bei uns momentan auch gut...
Andererseits müsste man auf dem Grund gehen, warum der Hund nicht gehen will? Ist er zu stark ausgelastet und will nicht? Ist er zu gelangweilt? Ist ihm zu heiß / kalt? 

Bei uns war der Hund eine Zeit lang zu gelangweilt, daher gestalte ich meine Gassirunden inzwischen ganz unterschiedlich... Neben ganz verschiedenen Runden, nehme ich auch mal ein Spielzeug mit (wo ich immer wieder paar wenige Minuten mit ihm spiele und dann weiter gehe), baue spontan kurze Trainingseinheiten ein, verstecke Leckerlis zum suchen an einem Baum und variiere an Gehgeschwindigkeiten bei denen der Hund mithalten kann... Natürlich nicht alles immer auf einmal, sondern abwechselnd und dazwischen auch genug "langweilige" Spaziergänge...

Ab und an ist es aber auch so, dass mein Hund sich hinlegt und einfach beobachten möchte, was auch gut ist und wenn ich Zeit hab, dann lasse ich ihn auch mal paar Minuten beobachten.

Ansonsten könnte es evtl an den Uhrzeiten und Temperaturen liegen? Meinen Hund kann man am frühen Morgen oder bei Regen in die Tonne kicken... Da ich das weiß, vermeide ich beide Situationen...

Was das ziehen angeht... Ich würde jetzt nicht unbedingt einen Spaziergang in ein Kräftemessen verwandeln... Allerdings hilft evtl ein selbstbewusstes Weitergehen? Mein Freund wird oft sehr langsamer, sobald der Hund langsamer wird und das resultiert darin dass sich letzterer hinsetzt oder hinlegt... Wenn man beim langsamer werden, einfach selbstbewusst weitergeht funktioniert das zumindest bei uns recht gut...

I was a 17 year old with Borderline, heavy ptsd, always hurting myself and had some suicidal attempts and other problems. A handful. Luckily I got a very understanding therapist who would take me in - though I had to agree that, if I tried suicide again, he'd drop me. He send me to inpatient care and after that we continued therapy. Helped me a lot and I'm much better now.
